utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Hayden, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we please have again 65 ter 00769, and paragraph 4.1, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, as you can see on the screen when we adjourned yesterday we were talking about paragraph 4.1 of your report in front of you. Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 4.1 you mentioned that you arrived at the Knin cemetery about 1530 and you were accompanied by the -- Cermak, the agent officer and also an unidentified colonel described as a -- as an information officer. Now, this information officer, where did he come from; do you know? Did he join you there, did he came with you from General Cermak's office or can you maybe assist the Court with that, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure where he actually came from, but he joined the liaison officer at the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And as you indicated in your statements, you didn't get his name although you made a sort of description of him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, it is also clear from your statements that you -- at that time and it appears it was sort of towards the end of your mission, that you also had certain questions in your mind and in fact you asked this information officer some questions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, before we go to the specific questions that you put to him at that stage, maybe if we can maybe just go back to your report that you prepared just to maybe to highlight or clarify some issues before we deal with the specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: So if I can, please, Mr. Registrar, ask you to go back to page 3 of the report, paragraph 1, please. And, Madam Usher, maybe required we provided you with copies of the statements and also the report. Can it be provided to the witness if he requires them. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, as can be seen from paragraph 1 of the report it appears that you made certain headings and discuss certain information that you were provided under these headings of the report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, the first heading, as we can see, deals with systematic burning and looting. Now, if I can refer you and maybe just refresh your mind with regard to paragraph 1.1 of this report it appears from the paragraph 1.1 that a lot of the information except the last sentence that I will deal with was provided to you by other people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the last sentence or the second-last sentence of paragraph 1.1 it appears that on the 17th of August you in fact visited the area of Kistanje as you pointed out there and it appears that you personally witnessed some of these incidents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for references purpose, it is also referred to paragraph 10 of the statement of the witness P-987. Now, if we can, Mr. Registrar, just move quickly to the next page, paragraph 1.6, please, just because it is linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, if you look at the first paragraph there, paragraph 1.6, the mission noticed in Kistanje that the only undamaged building was the orthodox church. Now when you witnessed that, was that also part of the mission that you went on, on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And then, as a result of the information that you obtained during this mission, did you then, on the 19th, ask the colonel about that incident?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, what did you ask him and what was his reply?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not ask the question. One of my colleagues did. I was standing with him when the question was asked, and the question was in regards to the undamaged church in the village of Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And what was the answer?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The colonel replied, We don't want to be seen like the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And what did you sort of make from that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it was a curious response and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness was present when this was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may explain to us how he understood the answer that -- first of all, what the answer was, and then, second, how he, at the time, understood the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My objection is pointed to any conclusions that he is going to articulate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask -- we'll ask the witness how he understood at that time the answer, what came to his mind, how he interpreted that answer. Whether that is a conclusion which has any merit is still to be seen but we want to know how he understood it at the time. Please, could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context of what the mission had been doing, and what we had seen in the area, in and around Knin, I felt that the answer was indicative of sort of a public relations act. The colonel was informing us that, Look, we protected a religious building and prevented it from being damaged. However, all the other buildings in and around the church were damaged, so we were concerned that not enough effort was being made in regard to controlling or limiting or stopping the destruction of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we go back to 1.2, please, on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, it appears from sort of the -- I would call the first half of that paragraph, that you provide the reader with a lot of information about the villages et cetera, et cetera. Is that information that you sort of personally obtained or was it -- or were you informed about it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A combination of both. It was information received from UN personnel, as well as our own visits to these various villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: If I can be maybe more specific if we move to sort of the -- the middle of that paragraph, where it begins with the words and I quote: "During movements through the area mission members witnessed numerous houses in the final stages of burning while driving through Knin to Drnis on 18th of August." Then I will skip and then you: " ... returned on the 19th of August?" Is that sort of an aspect of an area that you personally witnessed and observed as part of your mission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to paragraph 1.3 there, please, you indicate there in the second sentence that in, and I quote: "In movements through the city by car and foot the mission saw that Knin had been systematically and completed looted. The majority of the damage was caused by the looting." Is this something that you also personally observed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And can you maybe give us an indication as to when did that happen. Was that -- give a date, was it on the 17th or the 18th or the 19th. Can you still recall?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three day, as we were in and around Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, the last sentence on paragraph 1.3 you talk about the preliminary assessment of damages to houses. Is that also information that was provided to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, it appears that information may be emanating from P64. If we can move to the next page, please, paragraph 1.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: There you mention, and I go to the second line of the paragraph that the mission spoke with people in. Can you -- can you perhaps inform us who these people were?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons were displaced individuals who had taken shelter at the UN compound who we spoke with and who had been residents of Knin at the time that the offensive took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And then the last sentence of paragraph 1.4, and I quote: "Mission members saw on numerous occasions soldiers driving civilian vehicles without licence plates loaded with goods from both houses and stores. " Did you also personally observe this?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record purposes, further information on this appears in paragraph 14 of the witness statement, P987.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, if we can move to paragraph 2 on that page. It appears that you in fact interviewed some of these people and the information that you put down there, you received from these people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Next page please paragraph 5 -- page 5, paragraph 2.1.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: It also appears that you interviewed some people and then you put down the information that you received as the result of these interviews. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Next page, page 6, please, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: There you talk about civilian casualties and missing persons and in paragraph 3.1 of the report you talk about that General Cermak gave you a full list. Now, the lists that you are talking about, did you receive them at the meeting that you had with him on the 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Next page, page 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, you now deal with another topic, the mass grave in Knin cemetery and we already dealt with that and you informed us about the question that was put to this information officer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit, as far as the numbering of pages is concerned, can we just look at the English at the bottom. Madam Usher, could you assist us. The page we're on, could we see the bottom page numbering. Yes, you're referring to pages which is apparently the sequential numbering of the pages in the electronic document although the page numbering in the hard copy is always one less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: That is so. I thought -- you're absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So people do not start getting confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then move to paragraph -- page 8, paragraph 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: There, Mr. Hayden, you refer back to basically three meetings that you had with -- with persons identified in paragraph 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3. Were you present during this interview and is this a fair reflection of what happened during these interviews?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Then if we could move to the next page, please, page 9, paragraph 5.4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: This also indicates that you had discussions with UN personnel on the 17th to the 19th of August, and there you inform the reader about the conversations you had with these people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And can we move to the next page, please, page 10, and specifically paragraph 5.4.6, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: If I can just refer you to the last sentence, Mr. Hayden, and I quote: "The HV colonel stated that the intent of the shelling was specifically to create a disorganised mass panic and exodus of Serbs." Now, firstly, this HV colonel that you referred to, was that the same person that you met on the 19th of August or was it a different person?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And who posed this -- the question to him; can you still remember?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And what did you make from the answer?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it confirmed the information received from the UN officer that we spoke with, the Senior Military Observer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Objection to what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you, at that time, develop any thoughts on what this answer would mean? And, if so, please tell us what thoughts you developed at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HV colonel's answer was similar to other answers I had received in conversations with people that we had interviewed during that period of the 17th to the 19th. And in addition, it seemed to confirm information that we had come across prior to our arrival through print and electronic media, and the impression that I had, based upon this various information, was there had been a very particular use of -- of artillery in the offensive, designed not so much to destroy or damage but to cause a panic effect amongst the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can just refer to paragraph 6 just lastly: "Sector North Krajina." This is information that you received after you had sort of terminated the mission. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I request that this document be admitted into evidence, 65 ter 769, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has a new version been uploaded in which any reference to Mr. Hjertnes is removed? And has this been shown to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: We haven't uploaded it yet, but we've discussed it with the Defence this morning, Your Honour, and we've agreed that regard to paragraph 5.4.6 everything will be redacted expect the last sentence that I just read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: If that is agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I consulted with counsel prior to that time and I think that in a review of the document that is agreeable. So subject to our prior objections on this, that's agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You agree that the instructions of the Chamber were followed by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as far as redactions are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now then where does it start, Mr. Du-Toit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: It will start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we start reading? You said from the beginning so it is in a conversation with, that is where the redaction starts, up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Up till the -- we thought, you know, up till the sort of the information officer which is inverted commas, until then. It is sort of second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: -- third part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you -- that sentence starts with: "His impression." Now if you start there, it may be totally unclear who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: That's what we discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Although it is in his statement also but we felt maybe you know that -- you're quite right because the information was confirmed and that is why the question was asked, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My understanding is that if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Kehoe please speak in the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding on that paragraph was everything out of there except the last sentence on paragraph 5.4.6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what we then would -- what then would remain is the HV colonel stated that the intent of the shelling ... that's where we start reading again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And from the answer just given by the witness, we understand that the HV colonel is the information officer which is mentioned in the previous sentence, which is taken out, which is the same person as he referred to earlier in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- so then the redaction, with this clarification on the record, should be everything apart from the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would add that section 6 deals with Sector North which is not part of the indictment, and I would suggest that that section be redacted as well. I have no idea why it would need to remain in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm only rising because I dealt with the objections yesterday. I don't think they should be seriatim. We consulted with counsel this mourning with respect to the issues raised yesterday and I would suggest that the document be tendered as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it or is it not part of the indictment? Sector North is not part of the document. It should not be in the document. It is pretty simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not as simple as that, Mr. Kuzmanovic, if something is not part of the indictment. Bosnia is not part of the indictment either. I mean, sometimes have you some background information. We'll look at, but I -- the Chamber will consider whether -- where it stops that we can add objections to documents that were submitted on the 23rd of September. We'll consider that. Mr. Du-Toit, perhaps you wait a moment with uploading so that the Chamber will first consider whether paragraph 6 of the report is in need of further redaction and then only then uploaded. Then we also will not decide on admission at this very moment because we would not know what we are admitting. The document, the redaction in paragraph 5.4.6 is clear. The Chamber will further consider paragraph 6 and for the time being, the document remains MFId. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, I was -- just brought to my attention will you also provide a number later or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I do agree that to have it marked for identification it needs a number. Otherwise there is no mark. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes exhibit number P988, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, we just dealt now with this report that you prepared dated the 25th of August, 1995. Can you please inform the Court whether this was the first sort of type of report that you prepared dealing with aspects like this or did you had any other experience of preparing similar reports dealing with other situations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have had experience preparing other reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can you perhaps enlighten the Court on that, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, previous to this mission, I had been in Serbia where I had been working with the Serbian Helsinki Committee on the question of Kosovo and spent several weeks there interviewing prisoners, Albanian Kosovar prisoners in Kosovo and preparing a report on their mistreatment by Ministry of Interior personnel. And prior to that, there had been work on the -- the conflict in Chechnya which included a fact-finding mission and in which -- in which we examined similar questions as we did in the report on the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with the knowledge that you had in preparing this report that was just marked for identification, can I please take you back to the second statement that you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, it's Exhibit P987. And can we please move to paragraph 18 thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hayden, can you just please have a look at paragraph 18 of your statement. There you deal with observations and conversations, et cetera. And then it appears from the statement, first, that in paragraph 18 and in paragraph 19, and paragraph 20, and then moving on to the next page, that you basically provided four basic reasons why you came to that conclusion that you mentioned in the beginning of paragraph 18. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, correct me if I'm wrong. Is what you state in paragraph 18 to 20 a type of summary of your observations that you talked to us about, what you observed and what others observed in the report that we just had?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can I perhaps just ask you one question on paragraph 19 of your report -- of your statement, especially the first sentence thereof. If can you just read that, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Second, the fact that the initial artillery barrages focussed on a small number of targets rather than wholesale bombardments indicated to me that a strategy was sowing terror and intimidation was used rather than full military engagement with Krajina Serb troops or unlawful and wanton military acts against non-combatant civilians."

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can you -- can you perhaps just explore with the Court what do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: -- mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit, would you be so kind to check or find out whether the French translation is finished because a small pause when the translation is ongoing does not help the interpreters fully out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: I apologise. I will do so. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can you please answer that question, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you restate the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can you perhaps elaborate on what you understood or what you meant by this sentence that you just read out to the Court.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understood was that the artillery barrage, barrages or the artillery was not used to target whole areas, villages in particular, or civilian areas, buildings in these villages that we visited did not evidence the type of damage that would be caused by artillery shells or in fact any other kind of combat versus damage that would be caused by that, and it was readily apparent that the damaged buildings that we saw were destroyed after combat activity had ceased in these areas. The buildings exhibited, you know, all of the hallmarks of having been burned from the inside with some material other than having been first hit by an artillery shell, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Now, in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask a clarification of this answer, Mr. Du-Toit. The line you read, the sentence you read was about the way in which artillery was used and what the purpose of this use of the artillery was. Asked to explain this, you explained to us that houses were apparently destroyed not through artillery. Now, that doesn't explain much of what you read, because that was about how artillery was used and for what purpose it was used. So the answer is maybe an impression you may have gained but has little to do with what you read, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe my answer -- my answer spoke to the physical destruction that we witnessed, true. As to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are talking about, at least you read in paragraph 19, in what way the artillery was used, and, therefore, I'd like to hear from you rather an explanation of what you read than an explanation of how you assessed the damaged apparently not inflicted by artillery. You said: "Initial artillery barrages focussed on a small number of targets." Could you explain what targets and what the source of knowledge for this statement is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the information that I gained in my conversations with particularly UN personnel, military personnel, and information gained in pre-mission research and then the visual evidence that we saw on the ground all came together in a way to give me the impression that the artillery had been used tactically not to destroy physical structures. Hence, it was used against limited selected targets. I may not -- I do not know exactly which targets. They may have been specifically military targets. It could have been an open field next to a village, but the intent of the use of the artillery was to cause panic amongst the civilian population and even amongst the military of the -- of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand your answer. You include the possibility that the small number of targets were military targets. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do include that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, you apparently gained the impression that this was to cause panic among the civilian population. Could you explain to us how a focussed targeting of military targets -- what makes you then believe that this was intended to -- to cause panic among the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the -- not just military targets, but I think that military targets were included and non-military targets. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about what you know about the non-military targets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were locations in Knin or in other areas where -- located adjacent to villages where the artillery shells had landed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an example where you -- did you observe that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not observe it but you could see the holes left in the ground from the explosions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any place where you say, We saw not one impact but artillery impacts close to villages where the village itself was apparently not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we saw that in a couple of villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember which villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember which villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a follow-up question regarding also paragraph 18 of the report where you talk about that the burning and looting were systematic and coordinated. Can you perhaps enlighten the Court as to the basis for that conclusion that you reached, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and my mission members reached that conclusion based upon the scope and scale of burned buildings in the villages that we visited during the time of the mission. In many cases an entire village would have been completely damaged by burning caused not by combat, and in certain cases, these -- when we looked inside these buildings we could see that they were completely emptied in many cases with nothing but the debris of the roof and some of the internal structure having fallen inside the building caused by the burning. Given that there were so many buildings that we saw exhibiting this sort of damage, we could only come to the conclusion that there had been an organised effort in which individuals were given the material means to burn buildings as well as to take personal possessions out of these -- these buildings prior to them being burned. And the fact that we saw a number of private vehicles, as indicated in the report, without licence plates, and filled with various kinds of possessions being driven by uniformed members of the Croatian military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I ask a few clarifications here. Paragraph 18, you say that: "Buildings that had been owned by ethnic Serbs were marked for burning." Could you tell us how they were marked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these buildings either had been marked with a rough outline of the Serb Chetnik hand signed or had been spray-painted or marked in such a way that indicated it was a Serbian house in -- to distinguish it from the Croatian houses that had been marked with the phrases mentioned in paragraph 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the houses were completely burned, would it still be visible that they were marked with spray paint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many of the houses were not let's say completely burned to the ground given the common building materials. But all of the -- in particular the wood components of the structure would have burned and collapsed inward, leaving exterior walls still standing in which you could see these words or images painted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Another question is: How -- from the pattern of destruction, how can you conclude from that, that people were provided with the material for burning? I mean, how can I see from the level of destruction that people were provided with material to cause this to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it seemed quite reasonable that in order to undertake burning so many physical structures that you couldn't just walk up with a box of matches in your pocket and -- and sort of arbitrarily go to town. These -- these buildings would have had to have been burned using some sort of fuel or accelerant and given that -- given that fuel was of short supply in that region, it would have required that persons who conducted this either brought it with themselves from outside the region or were given the materials to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Brought from outside or given to them. There's a lot of reasoning in -- Let me just -- let's just assume it was one or two litres of fuel left in a house, in many houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm. That could be possible too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would completely undermine your conclusion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. It may have just made the job easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say on the basis of the pattern of the destruction it must have been that they were provided with material. You even add to that that due to the shortage it may have come from outside the area. And then you say, Well, if there was fuel in the houses it may have made it easier for them. Now let's just assume that the shortage caused that no one could provide them with any feel and that limited fuel was found in the houses, would that not undermine your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I would think that, yes, if there were additional fuel or fuel discovered, that would have made the job easier. But, again, I don't think these individuals took much time, in terms of exploring the interiors, for instance, to find the fuel first that might have been left behind or hidden away somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is what you discussed with the -- your sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would discuss with them how much time they took and whether there would be fuel avail in the houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these are conjectures about how things would have taken place. Thinking it out in terms of, well, if they -- if ex-Croatian personnel decided to burn this village, how would they go about doing A, B, and C, with what materials and in what time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Du-Toit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, can we move to paragraph 7 of your statement, please. It's page 3. Last sentence there, Mr. Hayden, if you can just and I quote in inverted -- : "Although I had heard about an evacuation plan organised by the Croatian -- Krajina Serb political administration prior to the offensive" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Du-Toit, did the Chamber not instruct you to take out paragraph 7 in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the version that we filed last night in fact exclude parts of paragraph 7 and that was sort of the middle portion of -- of paragraph 7. That's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking what you did. I'm asking what our instructions were according to -- and I'll just check that in yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Then in the 2004 statement, paragraph 7, in its entirety, is not admitted into evidence." That is what I see on page 10578, line 12. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. And I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the redactions would be in accordance with admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. My -- I -- I can't speak specifically to what communications were made with Chambers but what we noted was and had intended certainly to communicate it to Chambers that in the -- the suggested redactions were clearly focussed on a particular type of evidence and for a particular reason so we -- and we noted that the redactions suggested for the other statement focussed exclusively on the Hjertnes aspect and left intact the reference to an independent source and we thought the same should be done with that and we had intended of course to communicate that both to the Chambers and to counsel fully, except the fact that the Court's specific instruction was with respect to the entire paragraph but we thought that's because the Court simply didn't see that one sentence in the midst of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that gave us carte blanche to go forward with the question but I think we had anticipated that it would in fact be resolved so that the redaction would be consistent with the source of the concern, which was the Hjertnes material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber decided on paragraph 7 because there was no such Hjertnes in the paragraph that we thought it better to take it out, which of course does not prevent you from eliciting any oral evidence which is not directly related to Mr. Hjertnes but since we specifically said that the whole of paragraph 7 would be taken out, I think it would not be good to ask the witness to read from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, can I just ask you that you also talked to people about whether there was or was not an evacuation planned. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: And if I can show you, please, Exhibit D137, please. Mr. Hayden, this is a document that you were shown yesterday and it appears to be a document signed by Mr. Milan Martic dealing with evacuation of people on the 4th of August at 1645 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Have you got any comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, myself and mission members did not see this particular document at the time that we were there. We did receive, in the course of our various interviews, information that seemed to indicate that there were -- had been some sort of statements regarding by -- by Krajina Serb authorities regarding an evacuation, an organised evacuation. Senior UN personnel that we spoke with stated that Krajina Serb authorities had approached UN personnel and requested fuel and vehicles to aid in an evacuation, but in the course of other interviews, it seemed to us, myself and the other mission members, that a -- an organised evacuation did not actually take place. That may have been because the Serbian authorities did not have the resources or materials to do so, and the timing in which the Croatian military offensive took place may not have given time for an organised evacuation, and, thus, we were left with the impression -- I was left with the distinct impression that the evacuation had been disorganised in large measure and -- and the Serbs resident in Knin and the other villages we visited were -- had to fend for themselves and to flee in any way necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is all I have for this witness. And thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Du-Toit. Mr. Kay, you will the first to cross-examine Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just want to follow up on your last answer, Mr. Hayden, because you were shown a document D137.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have it back on to the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exhibit D137 was dated the 4th of August, 1995, and did you appreciate who had signed that decision on that day?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The so-called president of the Republika Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, this wasn't a document that you had seen in your fact-finding mission, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But would I agree that it is an important document?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in the light of discovering new information, such as this, do you think you ought to reconsider the statement you made concerning the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for several reasons. One, we did interview a number of displaced persons from the area in the UN compound who stated that there had been no resources available for them to flee or evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just stop you there and we'll take it section by section.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those are of course the persons who remained?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we know that this is some 800 or 900 people that remained in the UN compound. How many people went missing, left the area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you -- of course you went on a fact-finding mission? I presume this is something that you would have considered.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I doubt at that time that the Croatian authorities or even the UN personnel in the region had a clear appreciation of the number of displaced persons who had fled the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, didn't you consider roughly how many people had left the area? After all, you were looking at the village, you were touring, you were making judgements as to whether there had been an evacuation plan or not, whether it was organised or not. Didn't you consider the numerical issues?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. But, again, we had no knowledge of the total population of the villages or the town of Knin that we visited. There were no documents that could have been provided, for instance, by Serb authorities regarding a census of the number of individuals who lived in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't do any research on this matter [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please for Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't do any research on this matter?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not specifically as to determine the total population of X, Y, and Z village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I thought this was a fact-finding mission?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't a census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, no, but it was dealing with clear issues and you were making judgements and writing a report about it. Do you consider that on this matter you had sufficiently informed yourself?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If 150.000 people had left the area and you saw a collection of 800, would that indicate a different set of circumstances to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, that there was a plan for people to evacuate the area.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. I do recall in the preparation to the fact-finding mission seeing electronic -- excuse me, electronic media, television images of people fleeing into Bosnia from the Krajina region, and these people were on foot, on horseback, in trailers being pulled by tractors, but there certainly were no images of buses, for instance, or Serbian Krajina military trucks transporting people from the region into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why would you have to go in some form of public transport for it to be part of an organised evacuation plan?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if a political authority is going to issue an evacuation plan, and in particular reference to this document you referred to, it's decided the evacuation shall be carried out in a planned manner according to prepared plans along routes, that would seem to indicate that not only is there a so-called plan with a map, but there would be additional resources, such as vehicles, to execute that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where does it say that in the order?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not, but one can read or infer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm going to ask you questions now about your mission. You went to the Knin area on the 17th and you left on the 19th. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You called in your statement of course the Republic of Srpska Krajina, which is one place it wasn't. Did you realize it was part of Croatia when you visited it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why did you call it Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because the political authorities who claimed to exercise authority was exercising their authority in the name of that political unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of Republic of Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. What time did you arrive in Knin on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early morning, around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And where did you go when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our first stop was at the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in the UN compound for?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a few hours, approximately. We were there, we attended a press conference and then had a variety of meetings with UN -- senior UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After those meetings at the UN compound where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We then proceeded to try to make contact with Croatian authorities in order to set up interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what else?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we began to move about the town of Knin, to visually see what had taken place. In the course of that, we would speak to, if we could, people who we came in contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And were you staying in Knin?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were staying in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did you leave -- Knin to go to Split?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would leave approximately 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. So you spent the afternoon in Knin walking about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not just walking about, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What else?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trying to set up other interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Moving about in Knin and in the outlying areas that we could visit in our vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On that day, you went to outlying areas?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is not a very big region so it's -- you can quickly move from the town of Knin to some of the outlying villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which outlying villages did you go to that day?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall which ones I went to specifically that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said you lost your notes about this visit in a flood.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the notes were destroyed in a flood, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did any one else have notes of this visit?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My other colleagues had their own personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you could have asked for those notes?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From those persons? It is it not my responsibility to ask for their notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you made your report did you just look at your own notes then?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. Each and every day that the mission members were working and we would return to our hotel in Split and spent several hours going through our notes, talking about what we had seen, discussing the implications of it and then making plans for the following day. In the course of drafting the report I relied upon my notes and my colleague's notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell me anything more specific about the -- the 17th, where you went, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, other than what is detailed in the report. We moved about and we saw damage done to the buildings. We noted that the civilian population was nowhere to be found, other than those few hundred people who had taken refuge inside the UN compound. We noted that the area was under the control of Croatian military and police authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the 18th, where did you go? What time -- did you go to Knin, first of all?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At what time did you arrive?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, approximately 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what did you do then on the 18th, when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We continued with our work. On that day, we met with the displaced persons in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you went back to the compound?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and we interviewed -- we spent several hours interviewing the displaced persons who were willing to come forward and speak with us --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about their experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And one of those included Mr. Pupovac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After speaking to the displaced persons in the camp what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had other meetings and then we went out and about again through Knin and moved to other villages that we hadn't seen the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just stopping you there with the meetings. What meetings did you have on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically which meetings. In a context such as that, it's difficult to set up meetings. You have you to, you know, try to chase people down, and they may not be where they're at. So it does take a bit of time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what time did you leave Knin to look at other areas around Knin?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly. We did have a specific time-frame that we could be out and about in that area, given the -- the regulations of the Croatian authorities at the time. You know, they were controlling the movements of civilians, so we would need to be on the road and back to Split on or before 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What regulations from the Croatian authorities were regulating your movements?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were under the impression that there was a curfew at night for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had been told that by police at a check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What regulations were there preventing you going anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What regulations were preventing you going anywhere you wanted.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, there weren't any specific regulations preventing us going anywhere. We asked that question. The authorities said that during the daylight hours we could move about, and they did recommend that we not go in certain places because they could not guarantee our security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your report and in your statement, you refer to meeting Mr. Pasic on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just check my --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You can take it from me. It's not something I'd make up.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right, we met with Petar Pasic, the Croatian political commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at what time was that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. I don't know exactly when that time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And for how long did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his office. What he was using as his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if that was in the afternoon, you weren't travelling very much around the area, if you'd been in meetings in the morning at the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, the area is not that large, so if we had set up a time for -- a specific time for this meeting, we may have had time to also move about and possibly go to another village and return for that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you do your visiting on the way back from Knin to Split?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you do your visiting of locations on the way back from Knin to Split.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were certain spots on the way, yes, that we could stop. In fact, there were -- one day when we were returning to Split from Knin, there was a house that was in -- in the process of being burned which hadn't been in the process of being burned when we passed that way in the morning. So our -- so we stopped and we took photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any other meetings on that afternoon of the 18th?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we -- we had -- we had some meetings with -- there was a UN human rights officer that we met with for a period of time, both before and after the interviews were conducted with -- with the displaced persons in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if would you not mind, you talked about taking photographs. Is this photographic material made available to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The photographs and other documents aside from my notes would be in the archives of the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights in Vienna, Austria. Unfortunately, the IHF is now closed due to the criminal activities of its accountant who over a period of several years was defrauding the IHF.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he didn't take the photographs, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I see that it would be difficult to get access.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be difficult to get access to photographs and documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether dates and times were -- which is sometimes possible, whether dates and times were included in the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Were the images time stamped, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the images were time stamped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we would have a look at the photographs we would know when they were taking if at least the clock in the camera would be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, yes. It's been several years since I have seen those photographs, over 13 so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you any recollection on the number of photographs you may have taken during these two days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not a rough estimate whether 20, whether 200, whether ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we -- we took many photographs, I took many photographs, at least several rolls of film. My colleagues also took photographs and so I can't give you an exact number, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the time when you still needed rolls to make photographs. It may be clear to the parties why I'm asking these questions because it might give an additional source of factual information, whereas we are struggling with the factual basis for what sometimes seem to be inferences, conclusions, and opinions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it the correct that the first Croatian personnel you interviewed was Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Senior personnel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you interview any other Croatian personnel --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- on that day on the 18th? I'm just dealing with the 18th.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th. I would have to refer to the report. In one village that we visited we encountered a group of Croatian soldiers who we spoke with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they gave us some information, basic information as to what they were doing and sort of the lay of the landscape and then they advised us just to be careful and that was the extent of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm dealing with this on the basis of Croatian authorities which is the phrase you use in your report and your -- your statement --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- rather than conversations with people --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- on the ground. So people who were in a position to give an explanation, if they could, Petar Pasic was the first. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you speak to any other person like him who was interviewed on that day?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He told you that the destruction was being carried out by civilians taking revenge.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On Mr. Du-Toit's numbering, that's number 8 of the report. Number 7 in the bottom right-hand corner. And this is an aspect in your report that you don't deal with in -- in any detail. About the civilians taking revenge.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. In the course of our movements, we didn't encounter any civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the course of your movements, you didn't encounter any soldiers looting and burning, as you said. But this was a matter that was brought to your attention but not something that you considered further?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we considered it, but we ruled it out as, I think a distinct possibility, given that the only people we encountered were Croatian military or police or Croatian civilian authorities, and at that time, we understood that Croatian civilians, people who had let's say formerly lived in these areas were not being allowed in just yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your answer because you said: "Well, we considered it but we ruled it out as I think a distinct possibility."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. We ruled that out, that civilians were roaming around, engaged in revenge burnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Forgive me for sounding a bit impertinent. But who are you to rule out anything on this? You were on a fact-finding mission.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had to exercise our judgment based on our professional experience and the focus and intent of the mission. We discussed this as a possibility, given that certainly revenge killings or revenge burnings were -- had taken place throughout the areas of the former Yugoslavia that were areas of conflict, so we discussed that. But because we discussed it doesn't necessarily mean we agreed that it should be a primary focus or that we would include it as an element of our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm just referring to your statement, which you've put in in evidence. I'm looking at paragraph 9, page 4, and I'm looking at the sentence there in the last -- the last sentence of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you would not mind, I'd like to seek clarification of the last answer, just for me to understand. Do I understand you said: "We discussed this as a possibility it being revenge burnings or killings also in this area at that time." And then you said: "But because we discussed it doesn't necessarily mean that we agreed that it should be a primary focus or that we would include it as an element of our report." Do I have to understand here that what you say, that we consider that this may have been the case but we didn't focus on that and we did not decide that it would be part of our report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. We considered the possibility of civilians. But because of the one, for instance, the road traffic between Split and Knin, which is the primary way to get there, there weren't civilians on the road travelling back and forth and that the very few civilians that we did see in -- in the area seemed to indicate to us that the burning and looting probably was not being undertaken by civilians, Croatians who may have previous lived there or were just going there for an afternoon of fun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What you're actually saying is that since we considered it not likely that this was the case, we did not pay a lot of attention to first explore that possibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I ask you this question in relation to one of the questions that were put to you earlier, which was the question by Mr. Kay whether you researched, and let me take you back. You were asked about how many people had left, and then Mr. Kay asked you whether you did any research on -- on how many people had left. He mentioned 150.000 compared to 800, as you may remember, and he said: "You didn't do any research on this matter." And then you said: "Not specifically to determine the total population of X, Y, and Z village." Now what unspecific research, so apparently not to the level of detail that you mentioned, did you do on the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're asking me what research we did?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to the population in the area? Well, there was very little information available for one thing. We relied at that time on information available through the media, focussing specifically on the events within this time-frame that we were looking at. There was information that we received from UN High Commission for Refugees operating in the area or the UN human rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What information did you receive from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Information regarding let's say that there are large numbers of displaced persons who are moving and require assistant, et cetera, et cetera, moving from Croatia into Bosnia. But there were no real exact numbers and I don't recall any specific numbers with respect to either the population prior to Operation Storm, nor, at that particular time when we were there, did we receive any specific numbers regarding the population that was there or people who had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking these questions for the following reason. The reason that you more or less, although not formally excluded for the possibility that civilians were looting is because as you said people had not returned, which of course leaves open how many people would have stayed in the area which did not have to return and were still civilians. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were in fact -- there was one incident, I recall, that there was a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm asking not about incidents. I'm asking you what your knowledge was about Croatians which had continued to live --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as we knew there were no Croatians who had continued -- you know, if we're talking about ethnic Croats versus ethnic Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- we weren't aware of ethnic Croats who decided to stick around. As I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that all ethnic Croats according to your information had left the area, well, let's say, somewhere between 1991 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as we understood I mean, many ethnic Croats had been forced out of that region or left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not talking about whether many left or not. But I'm talking about whether and if so how many had remained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. It wasn't an area of my focus for instance to understand how many ethnic Croats remained in the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, you draw far-reaching conclusions that civilians, Croat civilians out of revenge were not involved in looting because they could not have returned to the area. Now, that's the reason why I'm talking you to these details of the population because you -- if you do not know whether any remained and how many remained, it seems that your reasoning is registrar flawed, isn't it, because they could not have been involved because they had no opportunity to return is a flawed reasoning if there may have been Croatian civilians left in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we didn't see too many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking what you saw. I'm asking whether you agree with me that this is a considerable flaw in the reasoning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay. Yes, I'm looking at the clock. You're looking at the clock. We will have a break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could go back to Exhibit P987, the statement made in March 2004, and go to page 4 of that statement, which is the remainder of paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's the last sentence of that first paragraph of the page. "Therefore, it is my view that Croatian civilians or combatants dressed as civilians could have moved in following the primary phase of the offensive to undertake burning and looting operations in the area." Seeing that statement there in your statement, Mr. Hayden, in your mind, civilians were responsible, in part, for burning and looting operations in the area. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The word I used is "could have," which means that it is open to continued investigation or corroboration based on new information, so it's not an assertion that Croatian civilians did do it but could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, therefore, if that is a possibility, it is also a -- an aspect worthy of investigation by you and reporting by you in your fact-finding report. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been but the fact-finding report had a specific scope and a specific purpose. Time-wise we did not have the luxury to investigate many of the allegations or information that we received during the fact-finding mission, and we left that to the Croatian Helsinki Committee which continued after we left, their activities throughout the regions of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just looking at that sentence again, it says: "Croatian civilians or combatants dressed as civilians ..." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be the -- the old ploy of hiding your identity, military personnel dressing as civilians in order to do something that maybe they couldn't do if they were dressed in their military uniforms with their insignia clearly attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So civilians dressed as combatants would be exactly the same ploy?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it could have. You could insert that in there as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were a substantial number of reports at this time of civilians being dressed as combatants?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In writing "combatants dressed as civilians," do you think you made an error in your terminology?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could you assist me, then, as to where you found information of combatants dressed as civilians?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were two occasions that were relayed to us by UN personnel, a UN civilian police officer and a UN military observer, who said that they had seen Croatian military personnel engaged in the process of burning or destroying civilian property after the offensive had secured the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My question concerned combatants dressed as civilians. That was the question, and I'm interested in any information you could give the Court on that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a speculation on our part, based on what we understood to be the limitations placed on civilian movement in the area by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek to understand. Are you telling us that if someone looked like a civilian, he must have been a military person, because civilians were supposed not to be there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. But we didn't see many civilians in the area at the time that we were there, and the civilians that we did see and we had the opportunity to approach, identified themselves as authorities. I make reference to some civilians who were holding maps and we approached them and asked them what they were doing and who they were and they identified themselves as Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And we understood that civilians were not being allowed in yet into the region because of security reasons and it was still a war zone, and as we understood it, both from UN personnel we interviewed and from the Croatian authorities we interviewed, that civilians weren't being allowed to return as of yet until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now -- now you told us that you saw civilians with maps and you considered them authorities, and now you're explaining to us that civilians were, according to your information, were not allowed to enter the area.
