Did you see any people in civilian attire which were not using maps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I can recall, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So everyone in civilian attire was -- having maps and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- considered to be an authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm saying that there were very few civilians dressed in civilian clothes that we encountered. And in fact in all the villages outside of Knin that we visited, which are listed in this report, the only one where we encountered civilians were these individuals who were holding maps and when we approached them, they identified themselves as civilian authorities. In other village there is was no one to be seen at all, other than check-points along the road or in the instance when we were in one village and we were approached by a squad of Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now after this explanation, could you come back to the question that was put to you by Mr. Kay, that there were combatants dressed as civilians, because from your explanation until now, I -- from what you observed, apparently you say these were authorities, civilian authorities, I take it, or would you except the persons dressed as civilians having maps nevertheless being military or combatants or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not following the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will not insist on an answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let us just move to paragraph 11, where you refer to a VW transporter and two men in civilian dress coming around the left side of the house. Civilians or combatants, in your understanding, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to tell because one of them was armed. And as we know, the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia used a lot of irregular unit, paramilitaries, who may or may not have had a uniform or operated solely in civilian clothes. I had no clue. I certainly wasn't going to approach that individual with the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that something you -- you knew about, that the Croatian forces had paramilitary units when they took part in Operation Oluja?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I would say no, I didn't know whether the Croatian military was using paramilitary units at the time. I didn't see any information regarding the disposition of forces prior to Operation Storm or, let's say, the disposition of forces inside of the Krajina other than those that were referred to such as the 4th and 7th Brigades and the 6th Reserve Brigade. Now a reserve unit usually is comprised of civilians who, during peacetime are engaged in civilian activities and they may be called up to serve in a military capacity. And so maybe these were reserve soldiers who hadn't had the time or opportunity yet to put on a uniform or maybe they were told not to wear a uniform. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it your view they went around the highways and byways changing their clothes from civilian clothes to uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea whether they did that or not. I wasn't privy to when and how they changed their clothes and what they put on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's turn to paragraph 14. The second sentence: "However, I do recall seeing several civilian vehicles loaded with stolen goods being driven by uniformed men." So, taking that, "civilian vehicle," could be a civilian dressed as a combatant.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. But the vehicle that I was referring to here was also loaded with stolen goods. The licence plates were removed, and the individual with the uniform had identifiable markings although I couldn't identify what they were as he passed by and I recall that he passed by a group of other soldiers who were standing in the street and they all waved at each other and sort of cheered. It was -- there was an atmosphere of, let's say, you know, we just won a football match. So I would assume that they may have known each other or have been possibly from the same unit but whether he was a civilian dressed as a combatant, I couldn't specifically answer. Again, it could be a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I may just look at your answer, you refer to this being as single occasion but the statement says "several civilian vehicles." So several civilian vehicles is wrong?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When I made this statement in paragraph 14 I'm referring to, yes, during the course of our time there we saw several civilian vehicles being driven by persons in military uniform, and I just relayed in that one anecdote my experience of observing one civilian vehicle with a person dressed in military attire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And how do you know the goods were stolen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't look like he had just come back from the grocery store or the local Home Depot and it seemed to be stuffed full with a odd variety of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What if he was a refugee who had been dispossessed in 1991, returning to the area to equip the home that he had lost?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood it, again, those individual Croats who had been displaced from 1991 were not being allowed back in yet by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you're wrong about that, that there weren't civilians entering this area at this time, would that cause you to reconsider your answers on that matter?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. You know, there are many ways to drive into the -- into the area besides the main road that we stayed on, and certainly we weren't everywhere at every time observing every place. So, yes, there is an possibility that civilians could have been in some of these places, but I -- I do note, as earlier, that when we were driving around outside of Knin in the villages outlying that we did not encounter civilians who seemed to be returning to their homes. As I stated earlier, in the villages that we visited, they were completely depopulated, and we did not encounter anyone trying to set up their household.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, let us go further into paragraph 14 then, shall we, second-to-last sentence: "We speculate that the vehicles had probably been abandoned by Krajina Serbs during the disorganised evacuation and then appropriated and refueled by Croatian military, police, or civilians." Rather contradicts what you were saying that there were no civilians in the area, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, it -- it doesn't necessarily contradict. It allows for the possibility of that to be the case, because, as I said we weren't everywhere at every place. Let's say we saw one vehicle driven by one civilian or a person dressed in civilian clothes, one does not constitute many civilians returning to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It says civilians; it's plural?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, it's two. They were in the same car together. It still doesn't infer that there were civilians about. As I said we did not encounter in our movements around Knin or in the outlying villages any number of civilians just moving about, returning to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know if the train was running from Split into Knin?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to turn now to paragraph 15 on page 5, so over the page, and I'm looking at the last two lines of paragraph 15. And it's this: "The fact that the statements by the police that they tried to stop the burning were inconsistent with my observations." Well, first of all, what statements by the police that they were trying to stop the burning?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the -- in the report, in paragraph 5.3 interview with the Croatian civilian police chief in Knin an officer Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence, "When we asked the police chief if he knew about the five arson suspects the military were surveilling, he replied that he heard nothing about them," and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, how is that relevant to that remark the statements by the police that they tried to stop the burning?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not, not that they tried to stop the burning. It's that they made no efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your statement says: "The statements by the police that they tried to stop the burning," and I'm asking you who said that and when and what were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you're still referring to paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So it says here: "In conversations with the UN personnel who had witnessed such incidents and having spoken with the Croatian police about their efforts to stop the burning and looting, it appeared to me that no significant effort was being made." So, again, I'm speaking not only about myself but my mission members also, in the course of the work that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said it appears to you in conversations, it appears to you that no significant effort was being made to intervene, stop, investigate, or arrest persons involved in committing these crimes. And I want to know, because it seems that you were directly advised of this.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Want to know what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who told that you the police, Croatian police, were attempting to stop crime.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't -- no -- no police officer or, for instance, the -- the chief of police -- excuse me, the police chief and Officer Jukic made any indication that they were doing anything about looting. They referred to it as a military matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What about burning, because that was the --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Burning, yes, burning or looting yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Burning and looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and so --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so I understood that the police were deferring to the military since the region was under military control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, speaking to the military officers we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have to say this, are you just making this up as you go along?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Have you ever been in a war zone?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not here to answer questions. You're the one who is being questioned by me.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you have answered that and said you haven't made it up. Why isn't it in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my statement was an elaboration or expansion on certain questions that emerged when the -- the Tribunal was looking at this report. Not everything that we contained in our notes or looked at was incorporated into the report, and this 2004 statement -- yes, I might not have focussed on that. But I have stated that the area was under control by the military, and in talking with the political commissioner, Petar Pasic, Mr. Pasic certainly left us with the -- the impression that, you know, the civilian authorities weren't in control of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you think he was in charge of the police?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, there was no clear chain of command, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know what his job was?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what I understood, he said he was the civilian political commissioner and he's there to handle the political side of whatever affairs arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So what he had to say might have been important?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he made a variety of different statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But you just chose to reject what he said?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You didn't follow up what he said about civilians committing crimes. You made no research, you didn't see whether he was right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think we did, because we -- you know, we posed these questions again. You know, we can do nothing -- he said, I can do nothing. Let's see ... General Cermak said that well, you know, we've got five persons under surveillance and he left it at that. Seemed to indicate that they weren't expending much effort in doing anything. UN civilian authorities either military or the UN authorities, whether military observers or civilian, you know, they didn't think in the course of conversations that I had with them or my mission members had with them that there was any significant effort being made in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, in your trip, you didn't see any looting or burning by the Croatian military or the police yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So even given that premise, when you're on a fact-finding mission for three days, didn't you think that that was something worthy of investigation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Investigate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I stated, we were there from the 17th to the 19th. My colleague from the IHF offices in Vienna returned to Vienna and then the continued field work was carried on by the Croatian Helsinki Committee so follow-up investigations into these allegations, and we drafted the report with what we understood to be the appropriate qualifying language. I mean, we weren't preparing this for -- as a legal document. This was a document that we were directing at the OSCE in order to urge the OSCE, through its various mechanisms, to place pressure on the Croatian government to address these issues. So of course many of the things that are contained in this report do require continued investigation, and one can't come to a final concrete conclusion in a matter of three days in an insecure war zone in which your movement is limited and your access to information is primarily through oral interviews with the people that you're able to meet there on the ground so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I anticipate the translation is going on, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't following the French but they have finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll slow down. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So are you saying your document, then, was a political document to encourage those people within the OSCE to -- to take a part or play a role?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Can I add to that question -- statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify that the IHF is a non-governmental organisation whose primary purpose is to serve as the Human Rights watch dog of the OSCE and its participating member states of which Croatia was a member state, and in being a member, Croatia had obligated itself to abide by specific documents within the framework of the OSCE as well as its international legal obligations as signatories to the Geneva Conventions or the other human rights documents. So given that our primary purpose was to serve as the human rights watch dog of the OSCE we work very closely with the OSCE and its participating states to address issues of concern and so when we prepare a report such as this, we try to do as best we can under the circumstances and then work further to continue addressing these issues in consultation with other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you would agree that Croatia would be entitled to have a properly researched report, if it's a member of that organisation.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not entitled. The IHF is not obligated to give anything to the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just go to paragraph 18, and it's the second sentence there, where you -- we've already heard your explanation about systematic and coordinated but the sense: "First, the extent of the burning indicated that whole villages were selectively burned or at least all buildings that had been owned by ethnic Serbs were marked for burning."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How did you know that? You didn't go to all the villages.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're basing that from what we saw in the visits to the numerous villages in and around the Knin area and so we certainly could make a logical inference that if those villages were substantially damaged through burning and looting, then other villages in the occupied area could have befallen the same fate. We left that up to our Croatian colleagues at the Croatian Helsinki Committee who were doing field work, investigating these issues throughout the region, the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the statement: "All buildings that had been owned by ethnic Serbs were marked for building." And would you agree that that is not a remark that you were in a position to make?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I'm in a position to make that remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many buildings did you see with markings on them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of buildings, as I mentioned earlier where --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How man? Sorry. How many was the question, not a number, how many?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know and since I do not have possession of my rough notes, I couldn't actually tell you that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So from your answer, we're to take it that all the Serb houses in the villages that you went to, every Serb house was marked in that way. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I was clear earlier in stating that some houses had markings on them, including houses that had markings that said, you know, this is a Croatian house, don't touch. So, in answer to your question, no, not every building I saw had some specific marking on it, but many did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And then just that sentence also in this paragraph, paragraph 18: "I think it also highly probable that local Croatians who had been displaced during the 1991 fighting were employed in the arson effort." Leave the word "employed" for the moment because the focus of the question is this issue of "highly probable that local Croatians who had been displaced during the 1991 fighting." By that did you mean civilians?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be civilians; that's probable. They could be reservists; that's probable. But I think our main focus was attention to the systematic and thorough nature of what had taken place. So even if civilians had ultimately been responsible, theoretically, it still would have been the Croatian military authorities to put a stop to it. They would have been obligated, legally, obviously, to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You don't need an accelerant such as gasoline or diesel to light a fire, do you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you would not mind, I'm seeking clarification of one of the previous answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was highly probable that local Croatians who been displaced during the 1991 fighting, that they were involved in -- that they were employed in the arson effort. Now, I come back to the issue that we have dealt with before. On the one-hand side, you say civilians had not returned, were not allowed yet to return; and, at the same time, you say that you find it probable that they were employed in the effort for arson. How can I reconcile this probability with, at the same time, your testimony that there were not yet back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And, yes, Your Honour, I understand your question, and there is an distinction between the two, the distinction being that if civilians, civilian Croats were employed to do the burning that infers or implies that their employment, their use, was at the knowledge of or instigation by the authorities in control of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a different matter. You said they could not have been involved in looting because they had not yet returned and they were not allowed yet to return; and now you say they may have been returned but they must have done it under the authority of A, B, or C. You also understand my problems with -- in reconciling your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you, Your Honour, lumping all civilians into this group of displaced persons who then all of a sudden came back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or maybe there were groups of -- there were individual civilians who because of their political beliefs or their desire to take revenge, for instance, may have been approached or they themselves approached the authorities or had been used by the authorities? I don't know. These are all speculations or inferences that required investigation either by the Croatian authorities or, let's say, by the OSCE in the framework of the role it plays in the region. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now have several options: Either those who were displaced had not returned; or they had returned and you say it's speculation that it might have been with the assistance or under the authority of the Croatian authorities; and the third possibility is that they returned just by themselves, spontaneously and nevertheless you draw all kind of conclusions in whether they could or could not have been involved in looting, arson, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you will see, Your Honour, throughout the report and my additional follow-on statements I don't necessarily infer or state that, you know, displaced persons returned without the knowledge of the Croatian authorities to engage in burning and looting and then leave. In the villages that we visited there was no one there. Now, if these displaced persons had intended to come home to their own homes, and if their homes were in this village where we counted all the buildings burned, it seems highly improbable that they would return just to burn down their own house and then leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your conclusion, "I think it is also highly probable that local Croatians who had been displaced during the 1991 fighting were employed in the arson effort" --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- the use of the word "employed" is based on what evidence?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm using it first and foremost just as a verb. You know, to employ, not necessarily in a paid position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've just asked you what your evidence was, rather than any grammatical explanation --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- just what your evidence was?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just based on what I had seen and the information that we came across, and again I state it is highly probable. It is probability. It's not a fact. I don't assert fact that this has happened and I have X, Y, and Z documents to back me up. But based on what we have seen, what we have learned, both before and afterwards and again I make -- I made these statements in 2004, so certainly additional information may have come my way in the intervening ten years. But, again, I merely say "highly probable." It's highly probable, that, you know, local Serbs before they left burned those houses, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, what information could have come your way in the last ten years?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while I was with the IHF it could have been information obtained by our Croatian colleagues at the Croatian Helsinki Committee who made -- who undertook tremendous efforts to engage in field work and obtained quite a bit of information in the process to follow up on these events. So some of that information I was aware of, but the great bulk of it I was not. So you would have to refer to that the Croatian Helsinki Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, you're the one giving evidence and you're the one that has used the word, and I'm asking you to give me the information, if have you it. If you don't have it and you don't know, it's much easier, Mr. Hayden, just to say if you don't know something.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I still don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After a certain point in time I went on to different things pursuing my professional career. I didn't sit here and focus on this thing for the last 13 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, may I seek clarification of one of your previous answers. You told us about the probability of Croats being employed in the arson, and then you said and I did not fully understand that. You said: "But it's highly probable that, you know, local Serbs, before they left, burned those houses. I don't know." Did you consider this a probability, a high probability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We did not consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then I have difficulties in understanding this line it's highly probable that, you know, local Serbs, or did you say improbable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was just merely drawing a distinction in terms of probability versus fact and I'm only referring to the statement. So you know many things can happen in the realm of probability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, probability means, to me, that it is certainly more likely than not. That's what probability apparently -- so, therefore, if we say it is probable that Croats were employed in it and it is probable that Serbs may have burned the houses before they left, that's, for me, inconsistent if you say probability means more likely than not, because it can't be more likely than not that the Croats and, at the same time, be more likely than not that the Serbs did it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: War does funny things to people, but again I'm just referring to the -- as the attorney is to the defence, to that statement, highly probable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning to paragraph 20, the first sentence of the statement: "Third, the fact that no or little effort was being made by the Croatian authorities to intervene or halt the burning strongly indicated that senior military and civilian officials had knowledge of or were directly involved in ordering and coordinating the burning and looting." Did you make any inquiry as to what efforts and attempts the Croatian authorities were making to stop burning, looting, and crime in the region?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what steps did you take to find out that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, asking persons that we interviewed, and for instance, General Cermak said that they had five people under surveillance, they were watching them because they believed that these five individuals were responsible for all that burning and looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You're exaggerating that. He did not say that five individuals were responsible for all the burning and looting. That's not right, is it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, about these incidents he admitted that they were happening and that he had five suspects under surveillance, so yes, I'm being a bit ironic but at the time we heard this information, it leads one to think hmm, how could five individuals be responsible for all of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is not what General Cermak said, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that the witness answered that question already that that was not what Mr. Cermak said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The three people you spoke to, Mr. Pasic, General Cermak, and the police chief whose name you don't know, none of them denied that crimes were happening. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dealing first with the police chief, did you ask him what measures the Ministry of Interior, the MUP, had taken to try and assist him in relation to preventing crime happening in the region?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I asked him a question regarding to preventing crime in the region. I don't recall that. I may have, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, why not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that at this point we were interested in several other questions and towards the end we did get to discussing the arson, and the most important thing was that we felt when we added this into the report was that he had no knowledge about the suspects that the military was currently surveilling and that he seemed to lack awareness about any efforts to address the issue, because he certainly wasn't doing it. His focus was -- I'm not quite sure what his focus was at that time. I think maybe he was trying to determine that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, did you appreciate there's civil police and military police? Did you appreciate that there was civil police and military police?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that what the military police may be doing could be different from the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that a matter that you took into account?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wasn't a focus at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You came to Mr. Pasic in the afternoon on Tuesday, the 18th, and by that time, you were biased against the Croatian authorities, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And isn't that the reason why you did not complete inquiries and make research in relation to the background that the Croatian authorities could have explained to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of many orders being issued by the Ministry of Interior directing police administration chiefs and police chiefs to take measures to prevent burning and looting in the area?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't privy to those and the police chief never showed me any of those or our mission members any of those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you see the police chief for?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's see. Probably half an hour at most. These people were all busy doing their various duties and it's not like we could sit down with them for several hours at a time. I could appreciate, as you asked me earlier, that they had responsibilities to attend to and sitting down and meeting with us was not necessarily high on their list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In your records of the report, you show that your meeting with General Cermak commenced at 1500.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It seems that the meeting with General Cermak commenced at 1430 --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and lasted half an hour and then we met with the Croatian police chief for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you just stop there. What time was the meeting with the police chief?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the notes, it states 19 August at 1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just get this timing right as it may be material as to your position.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know from your report at 5.2, or Mr. Du-Toit's numbering, page 8 that the meeting with General Cermak was at 1430.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know from your report on the same page at 5.3 that your meeting with a Croatian civilian police chief in Knin and Officer Jukic was at 1500.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those meetings did not take place in the same building, did they?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we met the Croatian chief, police chief, not in the same building as General Cermak but outside that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And by that you mean you met him in the police station where the appointment was booked?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't exactly remember. I know that the meeting with General Cermak at 1430 hours did not take the entire time. General Cermak was busy; we appreciated that. We asked him some questions and then he had to get on. And he then -- he also was kind enough to extended the assistance of his liaison officer and another to go and visit the Knin cemetery and on the way out of the office to go there, I believe that's when we ran into the civilian police chief because we had been trying to set up a meeting and before going into the meeting with General Cermak I don't believe we had had a time but just the confluence we met, as we were leaving, he was coming in and we had an opportunity to speak briefly about some matters and then we got into our vehicles and drove no more than a few minutes up the street to the cemetery. So the distances were very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the meeting with General Cermak was under half an hour?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes. We weren't there that long, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you give him the impression that you were from the International Commission of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. That would have been a subterfuge and an embarrassment. We clearly identified ourselves as members of the International Helsinki Federation for Human Rights and the Croatian Helsinki Committee for human rights. Whether he took that to mean something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One of your -- were you speaking Croatian to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. My Croatian colleague was serving as a translator. And my IHF colleague, who spoke fluent Croatian, was not speaking Croatian in the context of the interview, so that we could -- the mission members could confer later in terms of translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you don't know what was said?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on the -- yes, I do know what was said based upon the translation of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it translated for you in the room?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought you were giving a different circumstance.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. So I would ask a question, my colleague would relay it to General Cermak in Croatian, he would ponder an answer, he would say his answer and then my colleague would translate the answer for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So who was the translator for you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been Petra Klein.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did General Cermak have a translator?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no. But we, you know, let him know that in -- in introducing ourselves here is my Croatian colleague and she will translate for me, for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was the man you called I think Captain Dondo, was he there in the meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in that period of time you were with him, he treated you perfectly civilly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He wanted to help you to see whatever you wanted to see?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He did not put any obstacles in your way or try to stop you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And as you said, you wanted to see the graveyard and he sent you Mr. Dondo with you to take you there?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The four reports that you said he -- he provided you, which were to detail deaths in the area and where people were located or -- or buried, can you identify those reports more specifically, as to what documents they were?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were lists with names and locations of where the body was found and where the body was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was that provided to help you to inform you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The lists were given to us because General Cermak stated that these were -- these were lists of the individuals who were interred in the mass grave in the Knin cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, you didn't know whether it was a mass grave or not, did you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, we didn't. I mean, it looked like a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But we did not know what was inside of it. We were relying upon the information that we had received from UN personnel, who referred to the grave site, and Croatian authorities who had referred to the grave site and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this another example of you having preconceived ideas about the Croatian authorities and developing a bias against them because you believed there was a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were following up on the fact that we had learned that there was a mass grave in the Knin cemetery. So of course we would like to investigate further and try to understand, and so when we arrived at the cemetery you could see what appeared to be a mass grave, fully dressed with crosses arrayed on either of the longitudinal sides of a rectangular area that was quite long. So one can then say, hmm, this is a mass grave. Now -- I'm not -- well, I tried to go into this with as neutral a position as possible in order to try to do the work appropriately. If I came in there with the attitude that I was -- that I disliked General Cermak or the Croatians, that would certainly prejudice my work, but did I not. I don't take sides, except for, you know, civilian victims, people who don't deserve to be harmed or have their human rights violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I hear what you say, but I'm interested in the issue of -- of your believing there was a mass grave because nowhere do you ever suggest that it was alleged to be a mass grave or something that you yourself had no knowledge about. You just assumed it was a mass grave. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked about the mass grave. It's a legitimate question, and General Cermak stated that there was a grave that had, as it is stated here in section 5.2 of the report, stated that at the time of our meeting there were 120 victims, 108 of those being members of the Republika Srpska Krajina army and that the rest were civilian casualties of the shelling. So if it is a mass grave General Cermak himself verified that to the -- to our satisfaction and then proceeded to provide us with lists that would help us understand that yes, this was a mass grave and these are the bodies that we found that are placed in that grave, and then when we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question first because -- let's take this in stages. First of all he never said to you that there was a mass grave. That's right, he never said that to you, did he?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall whether or not he used that specific phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it makes a difference, Mr. Hayden. It makes a difference, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily because if let's say I asked him about, we understand that this is a mass grave in the Knin cemetery, what do you know? And then he proceeded to tell us about the mass grave. Now, when you put more than one body in a grave site typically it's just called a mass grave. It is a generic term but -- I'm not using it prejudicially to, you know, accuse General Cermak of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if you could just give us your definition of a mass grave so that we know what you're talking about and others may make a decision whether you are right or wrong. But if you could just give your definition.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say my definition of a mass grave is a hole in the ground that has more than one body in it and then is covered up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So a single hole?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a single hole but the single hole could be of a small size or a large size. So, you know, that would -- how big that mass is certainly would be predicated by how big the hole is, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if I chose to be buried with my wife, would I be in a mass grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say typically you wouldn't be called a mass grave but we understand that in a war type situation when you have something such as that with more than one body in it, you may not know how many bodies are in it, that was the big question, that we would refer to as a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that your comments and remarks about there being a mass grave were very insensitive and caused a great deal of upset to people? Did you appreciate that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't witness any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that to Croatian people, when you're making an allegation that there was a mass grave and that they might disagree with you, that you had to be sure of your facts?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems to be an unusual question, but I was speaking about what appeared to be a mass grave. What do you know about it. I can't control whether someone is going to get upset about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So in the short period of time that you saw Mr. Cermak. You came in with allegations against the Croatian authorities and not seeking explanation. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What allegations did you make? Shall we just have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made no allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into General Cermak's office and stand up and point my finger at him and say, You have done this and you have done that, no. We went in and exchanged information. We asked questions about the situation on the ground. There were more specific questions regarding burning, arson and looting. We wanted to understand what General Cermak understood. We wanted to get a -- the position of the ranking military authority there. So when we asked or I asked the question about the mass grave it wasn't standing up and alleging. It was, we understand that there is a mass grave in the Knin cemetery, what can you tell us about that. And that seems to be a perfectly reasonable question and General Cermak didn't seem upset at all. In fact, he reasonably answered and provided us information and assistance to go and learn more about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: M. Kay, may I ask one or two questions. It appears that you have done with the details with the graveyard. Mr. Hayden, I'm taking you back to your answers page 69 where you are dealing with the information you received from General Cermak. You said we asked about the mass grave it is a legitimate question and General Cermak stated that there was a grave that had, as it is stated here in section 5.2 of the report, stated that at the time of our meeting, 120 victims, 108 of those being members of the Republic of Serbian Krajina army, and that the rest were civilian casualties of the shelling. You say so if it is a mass grave, General Cermak himself verified that and then provided you with lists. Now, what you said there about the 120 victims, 108 being members of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, I understood that as referring to the persons buried. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let me then take you to the report, 4.3. There were two rows of crosses. The mission counted 86 crosses, which is the number of bodies claimed by General Cermak to be interred in the grave site. Cermak claimed, it reads one line further down, that there were 84 military buried, 74 of them Bosnian Serb army soldiers killed during a counterattack, and two civilians who allegedly died at Knin hospital. Now, this seems to be the details Mr. Cermak gave you about those who were buried, whereas in 5.4, I think, it is not about -- oh, no, it was not 5.4; it was 5.2. "In response to our questions concerning civilian casualties, General Cermak stated that at the time of our meeting, there were 120 victims, 108 of those ARSK soldiers. He stated that the rest were civilian casualties of the shelling in Knin." Are you mixing up, at this moment, the information General Cermak gave you about the graveyard and about casualties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, obviously, I -- I confused the two numbers and which sections they are at. So, yes. 5.2 refers to civilian casualties or our question regarding that, whereas the information in section 4 regarding the mass grave, 4.3, refers to the information that General Cermak gave us regarding numbers and the lists. So just confusing the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I urge you to be very precise on the factual basis of your answers. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw the chief of police, could you recollect what his actual position was? Chief of Croatian police can refer to a number of different jobs.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we understood, as I understood, he was the police chief in Knin. So he would be the ranking local police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And when you saw him, did you ask him what -- what measures he'd been taking to -- to stop crime?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall if I asked him. Maybe one of my colleagues did, but I didn't ask him specifically about stopping crime. Our primary concern was the detention centre, which the local police were operating, and the detainees, and to find out some specifics with respect to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your statement, in paragraph 20, that they'd made little or no effort to intervene or halt burning, is actually based on no information that you sought from the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we did speak with the police chief regarding the burning, and included at the end what we thought was the important statement. Again, I'd have to refer to my notes which I unfortunately do not have, or my other colleagues' notes to determine whether or not we asked that question, but I don't recall asking or discussing crime at large, you know like everyday crime, shoplifting or stealing a cow or, you know, drunken driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How can you go on a fact-finding mission and not ask key facts such as that? You must recognise that that's a failure in your work.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why should it be? Again, if he's the local police chief I doubt he was really in a position to exercise his full authority, given that it was a military zone so the military and the Ministry of Interior would be responsible for that. So maybe that's information we decided not to include in here, given that we were concerned about the detention centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that the police chief came under the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that, you know, most law enforcement in Croatia falls under the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate this in fact was not a military zone?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't appreciate it. I understood it as being a military zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where did you get that impression from?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way that the military was in control of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You're just making this up as you go along, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you inferring that I'm lying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're completely wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that people were pouring into this region --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- at this time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Trains coming in --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- buses?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- people pouring in. If they were pouring in they certainly would have been evidence of them pouring in in Knin at the train station or buses, and likewise as I said earlier, we did not see any civilians, let's say, persons who were returning to their homes in the outlying villages. They were empty and we didn't see buses on the roadways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Unless of course you failed to go a sufficient number of places and to do adequate research. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kuzmanovic, you're next, but let's first have a break, I think that would be ... Could I get an assessment of the time you would need and then from the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope to be finished by the end of the day's session, Your Honour. I will press to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then Gotovina Defence. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have one moment just to consult with my client about an issue and just tell you when we come back after the break and I will have a direct assessment then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Because it will have no impact on today's course of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to have at the end of this session five minutes for further scheduling purposes. Mr. Kehoe, if you could give us already an answer on the question I put to you before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you may proceed. Mr. Hayden, you will now be cross-examined -- apparently have you a problem hearing me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Kuzmanovic, who is counsel for Mr. Markac. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If we could go to P986, please, first -- first page of the statement. Mr. Hayden, do you have the hard copies of statements in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is 15 May 1996. This was something in written form that you wrote in response to a request from the ICTY. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 1.1, you note that: "The duration of my mission to the Krajina was from 15 to 20 August 1996. The 15-16 were spent in Zagreb and Split." Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but Zagreb and Split are not in Krajina; they are in the Republic of Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DU-TOIT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, to interrupt, but I think we may have just the wrong statement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that we have the 2004 statement on the screen at this moment rather than the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Six, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If I gave the wrong exhibit number I apologise. I had it written down as P986.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones be switched off, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is this P986 or did I incorrectly identify it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is P986.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just I'll repeat again. Section 1.1 when you refer to your mission to Krajina you refer to two days spent in Zagreb and Split and Zagreb and Split are in Croatia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are in Croatia, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the 20th when you returned back to Zagreb again, Zagreb is not part of the Krajina; it's Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now you said the 15th and 16th were spent in Zagreb and Split. Please tell what you did in Zagreb on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 15th it was meeting our colleagues at the Croatian Helsinki Committee. We also met with members of the UN human rights team and discussed information that we had received from them prior to our mission, any updates that they wanted to give us and then we arranged for our air flight travel and some other logistics issues and then flew to Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So I take it when you were in Zagreb you did not speak with or meet with any members of the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you. Kindly slow down for interpretation. It is impossible to interpret this rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kuzmanovic as well to make short pauses between question and answer and answer and question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just put a sign on me, Judge. I have to remember that every time. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So in answer to your question, no, we were unable to meet with members of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, I take it you were in Split?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do on the 16th in Split?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see, we arranged for a vehicle and staying at a hotel and planning the -- the period of the 17th and through the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So if I'm correct the first two days that were in Croatia, you did not meet with any members of the Croatian government or Croatian authorities. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Then on the 17th, in the morning, you left for Knin?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you would return to Split that evening?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the same thing on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And again the same thing on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave on the 19th for Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We left that -- that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then on the 20th, you were in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you had a press conference there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And at that press conference, you announced, among other things, that you had thought there was a presence of a mass grave. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to state, Mr. Hayden, that the objective of your trip was to put political pressure on Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: An objective of our mission was to relay information to the OSCE and urge the OSCE through its various mechanisms to address these issues with the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, is it not, Mr. Hayden, that if you had gone on this trip and had concluded that the Croatian authorities were doing the best they could under the circumstances, it would have defeated the whole purpose of sending you down there in the first place, would it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's still so much that was unknown or not understood, and we certainly just couldn't leave it up to our hopes that these issues or concerns that had arisen prior to our mission would be taken care of by the Croatian government, by -- as the best they could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, in answer to a question posed by Mr. Kay during his cross-examination of you, at page 54, your answer in part, was that: "The document we were directing at the OSCE," meaning your report: "In order to urge the OSCE through its various mechanisms to put pressure on the Croatian government." You hadn't had a written report at the time of your press conference. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The -- P986 again, on page 3 of that report and it's section 7. Just waiting for it to get up on the screen, Mr. Hayden. First sentence of section 7 states: "Since I did not actually witness any HV troops or Croatian police engaged in the act of burning or looting, I would have been unable to witness any HV troops or Croatian police attempting to prevent such actions." So it's fair to state that in terms of what you saw, you did not see any looting or burning yourself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you mention again in your statement, P986, in paragraph 12 on page 4: "The number of HV troops and Croatian police in and around the Knin area were more than sufficient to have mounted an effort to stop the burning and looting of Krajina Serb property." Now, you earlier stated in your report that you did not see any acts of burning and looting. So, please, can you tell me what the significant of paragraph 12 is to you, since you did not see that occurring?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 12 is an answer to a question posed by Thomas Elfgren. He sent me a fax with a list of questions and I answered those questions. I don't recall what the question was, so -- that would have led me to frame my answer in the way that I did. So I'm assuming he asked me what I thought about that, and so if that was the case, I gave him my answer that I thought it was -- there were sufficient number of troops and police in and around the Knin area, there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What is a sufficient amount of troops and police?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were troops -- I can't give you an exact number, let's say, but when we would drive into Knin there were check-points, there were personnel on the streets. When we drove out into the villages we encountered numerous check-points on roads leading into villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I guess that would have been appeared to be working since you saw no burning and looting, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, all burning ing and lotting predominantly occurred prior to our arrival. It was one of the, let's say, instigators for the mission was information we had been receiving through our Croatian colleagues and seeing in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what efforts the Croatian government, specifically the police or the Ministry of Interior, took to try to control, stop the burning and looting that was going on?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one seemed able to give a clear answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, though?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any independent efforts to speak with anyone from the Ministry of Interior to find out what efforts were being undertaken?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we made an effort to interview -- try to set up meetings with the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb but were unable to, given the time-frame, and follow-on activities were to be undertaken by our Croatian colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you give us an indication of how much experience you have to tell us how many HV troops and Croatian police were more than sufficient to have mounted an effort to stop the burning and looting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, having served six years in the military, I had some understanding of -- of the military and its function and being -- having worked in these zones, seeing how troops could be deployed or the -- Ministry of Interior forces could be deployed, it would seem that if they were deployed similarly as when we saw them, particularly at those check-points that were located in and around villages that we passed through, they certainly would have seen burning buildings taking -- and could have taken some sort of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true, though, you didn't even ask the appropriate authorities what steps were being taken by them to stop the looting and burning because none of those questions or answers are contained in your statements or report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we spoke with General Cermak who we understood as being a military authority, and Petar Pasic who we understood as being the civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you spoke with them, but I'm asking you specifically you did not ask these people, Mr. Cermak, or Mr. Pasic, or anybody, what steps are you taking. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We asked what are they doing to address this or what did they do to address it since most of the burning -- most of what we saw had already taken place prior to our arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But none of that is contained in your statements or in your report to the OSCE. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we make reference to it in -- you know, for instance, Mr. Pasic, we asked what measures he was taking to stop these civilians and I said, I can do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I asked specifically, though, about the Ministry of Interior earlier.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't meet with anyone from the Ministry of Interior. I would assume that maybe Mr. Pasic had been appointed by the Ministry of Interior. He didn't necessarily give me his credentials and detail those so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could go to page 3 -- I'm sorry. So what roles -- I guess what roles people had, for example, like Mr. Cermak or Mr. Pasic or anyone in the area, you weren't completely certain about, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not absolutely certain about but we were taking at face value the information these individuals gave us or the information that the UN authorities gave us in terms of directing us to who we needed to speak to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So you asked the UN about that and you didn't ask the Croatian government about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I said, when we were in Zagreb we did not have the opportunity to meet or else we would have posed those questions among many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you decide to come to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not actually sure. Probably several days beforehand as we were discussing it at the IHF and deciding how to go about doing this and what resources we had available, et cetera, and the timing as it fit within our other obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden, when you are coming to a country on presumably a fact-finding mission, don't you think that it is imperative for you as a fact-finder before arriving at a place like Zagreb or Knin to set up meetings with the appropriate Croatian governmental authorities, especially in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go to P987, please, which is your March 15th, 2004 statement. Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of paragraph 5 the sentence begins: "The facts on this report are based on rough notes prepared by myself, along with the other members of the fact-finding mission." Now you have already told us that your notes were lost as a result of a flood. Were you asked by anyone to contact other members of your fact-finding mission to get their notes?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You had mentioned that you had taken rolls of photographs in the time that you were in Knin. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you made any attempt to try to track down those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Has anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor asked to you try to try to track down those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could put D137 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about this, Mr. Hayden, in cross-examination earlier, D137, being the evacuation order signed by Milan Martic of the RSK. Now, the order itself, you said you saw during your proofing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you aware that the -- were you made aware that the primary evacuation route from Sector South was through Otric towards Srb and Lapac as noted in the evacuation order, point 3?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you made aware that UNMO reports, specifically a report of August 14th, noted that through the Jordanian battalion position there were over 70.000 people that had gone through that evacuation route as of the 14th of August?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware that a number of people had gone through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that to you is not an indication of a planned, organised evacuation, that 70.000 people go through the same route, through the same check-point?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was -- I guess that it was a principal route in the direction away from the Croatian military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Into Bosnia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware that the -- for the evacuation that the ARSK actually sought the help of UNPROFOR command as noted in section 3 of the evacuation order?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And they actually asked for fuel. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM CURTIS HAYDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I make note of it -- it's made note of in the report that the authorities -- the RSK authorities had approached the UN authorities for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to refer to P988, which is your report, Mr. Hayden, please, the first page of the report with the heading Introduction. You had earlier said during either direct or cross-examination, I'm not sure which, that you weren't certain of the number of people or that you didn't have a figure or estimate of the number of people that left Sector South. In this particular -- or in the Krajina region, actually. In this particular introduction you note in the third, fourth line: "The Croatian government claims that it welcomes back to Croatia the 154.079," then it says an estimate as of 21 August 1995, "Croatian Serbs who fled in the face of the offensive from the Krajina." Now, where did you get the number the estimate of 154.079?
